word.partOfSpeech: indefinite article, and the number one

pronunciation.notes: It rhymes with English 'mine'. In German, ei always sounds like the English word 'eye'.

word.shortDefinition: The German word for 'a', which is also the number one.

intro.title: The smallest word with the most faces
paragraphs: You learned ein on your first day of German. It's three letters long and means 'a'. Easy, right?

Then you find out it has six different forms, that it also means 'one', and that sometimes German leaves it out where English insists on it. Ein causes more everyday mistakes than almost any other word, so it deserves a proper lesson.

etymology.title: Where it comes from
etymology.summary: Ein goes back to the old Germanic word for 'one'. English has the same word twice: it became 'one', and a worn-down, unstressed version became 'an' and then 'a'. German never split them, so ein still does both jobs.

cognates.note: a more distant cousin, from Latin unus

bonus.note: English 'alone' was built the same way, from 'all one'. And kein comes from an old phrase meaning 'not one'.

tables.title: Six forms, one pattern
tables.intro: Ein changes its ending depending on the noun's gender and its job in the sentence (its case). The highlighted endings are what you need to learn.

rows.label: Dative
rows.hint: to or for someone, after mit, bei, von

notes: Only the masculine changes between nominative and accusative: ein Hund becomes einen Hund. Feminine and neuter stay the same.
In the dative, masculine and neuter share the same form: einem.
Masculine and neuter nominative have no ending at all, so ein Mann and ein Kind look alike.
Learn this table once and you get more for free: kein, mein, dein, sein and unser take exactly the same endings.

keyTrap.title: The big trap: forgetting einen
keyTrap.explanation: Hund is masculine. When a masculine noun is the object of the sentence, ein has to become einen. Feminine and neuter nouns never change here, which is exactly why the masculine one is so easy to forget.

wrong.verdict: Hund is the object here, so it needs einen.

correct.german: Ich habe eine Katze und ein Kind.
correct.literal: I have a cat and a child.
correct.note: Feminine and neuter objects: no change.

commonMistakes.title: Jobs and nationalities
commonMistakes.explanation: German usually leaves out ein when you say what someone is. Add it back only when there's an adjective: Er ist ein guter Lehrer.

commonMistakes.title: There's no plural
commonMistakes.explanation: Ein means 'one', so it can't go with a plural noun. Drop it, or use einige (some).

commonMistakes.title: Saying 'not a'
commonMistakes.explanation: German has a separate word for 'not a': kein. It takes the same endings as ein.

commonMistakes.title: ein or eins?
commonMistakes.explanation: Before a noun it's ein. When you count, or when 'one' stands on its own for a neuter thing, it gets an s.

sampleSentences.german: Ich habe einen Bruder und eine Schwester.
sampleSentences.english: I have a brother and a sister.

sampleSentences.german: Ich wohne in einem kleinen Dorf.
sampleSentences.english: I live in a small village.

sampleSentences.german: Sie arbeitet mit einer Freundin zusammen.
Wir haben nur ein Auto, nicht zwei.
sampleSentences.english: We only have one car, not two. (Here ein means 'one', so you stress it.)

quiz.explanation: Mann is masculine and the object of sehen, so it's accusative: einen.
Mit always takes the dative, and Freundin is feminine: einer.

quiz.prompt: Das ist ___ Buch. (ein, eine or einen?)
quiz.explanation: Buch is neuter, and neuter never changes in the nominative or accusative.

quiz.prompt: Ich habe ___ Auto. (I don't have a car.)
quiz.explanation: 'Not a' is kein, never nicht ein.

quiz.prompt: How do you say "I'm a teacher" in German?
quiz.explanation: No ein with jobs: Lehrer for a man, Lehrerin for a woman.

memoryHook: Ein is 'a' and 'one' at once. Only the masculine changes for the object: ein Hund wohnt hier, ich habe einen Hund.
